issues.legal_issue: An appellate order is not ex parte, and need not be set aside for a fresh hearing, when the affected appellant was represented and heard.
material_facts: The appellant was already on the appellate record as a legal heir and had participated in the proceedings through counsel.
The High Court considered arguments made by counsel who had appeared for the appellant and written arguments filed on behalf of another party.
The High Court found that the appellant had received a full opportunity to be heard on the merits.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s order was not an ex parte order in law, and there was no basis to set it aside or remand the matter for reconsideration.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXXII Rules 3, 10 and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure did not require a remand in these circumstances: the appellant was on record, represented through counsel, and afforded a hearing. The Court found no justification for a fresh consideration of the appeal.

rule.if: civil_appeal_from_a_suit_judgment and appellant_was_on_the_record and appellant_was_represented_by_counsel and appellant_received_a_hearing

predicates.civil_appeal_from_a_suit_judgment: The proceeding was a civil appeal arising from a suit judgment.
predicates.appellant_was_on_the_record: The appellant was included as a party to the appellate proceedings.
predicates.appellant_was_represented_by_counsel: Counsel appeared in the appellate proceedings on the appellant’s behalf.
predicates.appellant_received_a_hearing: The appellate court heard the appellant’s side and considered the arguments presented on its behalf.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal arising from a suit judgment includes an appellant who is on the record, represented by counsel, and heard, the output is that a remand is not warranted.

issues.legal_issue: A property purchased in one family member’s name may be found to be joint family property when the evidence shows that joint family funds contributed to its purchase and the family continued to live together.
material_facts: The family had lived together when the father died and continued to reside together for years after the property was purchased.
The purchaser received insurance proceeds following the father’s death and acknowledged that those proceeds were used, along with other funds, to buy the property.
The insurance proceeds were received by the purchaser as nominee, but the other heirs were legally entitled to claim them under the law of succession.
The purchaser managed the family’s affairs, and the evidence supported the existence of a joint family.

The sale deed named the purchaser alone and did not state that she acted for the joint family; the Court considered this alongside the evidence of the family circumstances and the purchaser’s dominant role.
issues.conclusion: The property was joint family property because the evidence supported the finding that joint family funds, including the insurance proceeds, were used for its purchase.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 39 of the Insurance Act, 1938, a nomination identifies the person authorised to receive the insurance proceeds but does not confer beneficial ownership; the heirs may claim the proceeds under the applicable law of succession. The Court relied on Smt. Sarbati Devi v. Smt. Usha Devi, which applied that principle. The Court also treated the family’s common residence, peaceful relations, and use of family funds as relevant evidence of a joint family and the property’s character.

rule.if: suit_concerning_whether_property_is_joint_family_property and joint_family_existed and family_funds_were_used_for_purchase and (insurance_proceeds_were_used_for_purchase or family_lived_together_after_purchase)

predicates.suit_concerning_whether_property_is_join: The proceeding concerned whether property was jointly owned as family property or belonged solely to the person named as purchaser.
predicates.joint_family_existed: The evidence showed that the family lived and managed its affairs jointly.
predicates.family_funds_were_used_for_purchase: The evidence showed that funds belonging to or available for the family contributed to the purchase.
predicates.insurance_proceeds_were_used_for_purchas: Insurance proceeds received by one family member after another family member’s death were used to purchase the property.
predicates.family_lived_together_after_purchase: The family continued to live together in the property after its purchase.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns whether property is joint family property, the family was joint, and family funds were used for the purchase, supported by use of insurance proceeds or continued family residence, the output is that the property is joint family property.

issues.legal_issue: A Hindu widow who is not a coparcener cannot act as the karta of a Hindu undivided family, but may manage its affairs as guardian of its sole surviving minor male coparcener.
material_facts: After the father’s death, his son was the sole surviving male coparcener and was a minor.
The son’s stepmother actively and dominantly managed the family’s affairs, while the son’s natural mother played a submissive role and did not oppose that management.
The stepmother’s role was consistent with acting as guardian of the minor coparcener rather than as karta in her own right.
issues.conclusion: The widow could manage the family’s affairs as guardian of the sole surviving minor male coparcener, although she could not assume the position of karta.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished the role of a manager from that of a karta: a Hindu widow is not a coparcener and cannot act as karta, but the mother of a minor male coparcener may act as his legal guardian and manage the family’s affairs in that capacity. The Court relied on Sushila Devi Rampuria v. Income Tax Officer and Dhujram v. Chandan Singh, and distinguished Commissioner of Income Tax v. Seth Govindram Sugar Mills Ltd. and Controller of Estate Duty, Madras v. Alladi Kuppuswamy. The Court noted that the position remained unchanged after the 2005 amendment to the Hindu Succession Act.

predicates.hindu_family_management_dispute: The proceeding concerned management of a Hindu family and its property.
predicates.sole_surviving_male_coparcener_was_a_min: The only surviving male coparcener was a minor when the family needed management.
predicates.widow_managed_family_affairs_as_his_guar: A widow managed the family’s affairs in a role attributable to guardianship of the minor coparcener.

issues.definition: When a Hindu family management dispute involves a minor sole surviving male coparcener and a widow managing the family as his guardian, the output is that she may manage as guardian but not as karta.

issues.legal_issue: A later suit is maintainable when earlier suits concerning the property were dismissed for failure to pay the required court fee, subject to the procedural rule permitting a fresh suit after rejection of a plaint.
material_facts: An earlier suit seeking relief concerning the property was dismissed under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for failure to pay the required court fee.
A later partition suit was also dismissed under that rule for the same procedural failure.
A separate possession suit had been brought under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act.
The suit under appeal was a later suit seeking injunction and, alternatively, partition.
issues.conclusion: The suit under appeal was maintainable under Order VII Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Order VII Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits presentation of a fresh plaint after rejection of a plaint, subject to the applicable procedural requirements. The Court held that the earlier dismissals for non-payment of court fee did not bar the later suit; the separate possession suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act did not alter that conclusion.

predicates.later_suit_concerning_property: A party brought a later suit seeking relief concerning property that had been the subject of earlier litigation.
predicates.earlier_suit_was_rejected_for_nonpayment: An earlier suit was rejected because the required court fee was not paid.

issues.definition: When a later suit concerns property and an earlier suit was rejected for non-payment of court fee, the output is that the later suit is maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: The apportionment of shares in joint family property may be upheld when it follows the established ownership finding, the parties’ succession interests, and the relief sought.
material_facts: The High Court found that the property was joint family property and decreed the plaintiff’s claim for partition.

The High Court allocated three-quarters of the property to the plaintiff’s side and one-quarter to the contesting defendant, taking account of the interests attributed to the family members and a will concerning part of the property.
The Supreme Court found no illegality or infirmity in the High Court’s apportionment.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s apportionment of shares was upheld, and the plaintiff was entitled to seek partition of the joint family property.
issues.legal_principle: Once the property was correctly found to be joint family property, the plaintiff was entitled to seek partition, and the Court found no basis to interfere with the allocation made in accordance with the relief sought. The judgment does not identify a separate statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this conclusion.

predicates.partition_suit_concerning_joint_family_p: The proceeding sought partition of property claimed to belong to a joint family.
predicates.property_was_found_to_be_joint_family_pr: The property was found to be jointly owned family property.
predicates.shares_were_apportioned_in_accordance_wi: The court allocated shares in light of the parties’ interests and the relief sought in the suit.

issues.definition: When a partition suit concerns property found to be joint family property and the shares are apportioned in accordance with the parties’ interests and relief sought, the output is that partition and the apportionment are upheld.
